voice.text: The sky over Dorothy's Kansas farm turns green-grey and still. [pause] Uncle Henry checks the tools on the barn wall and says: <emphasis>storm's coming</emphasis>. [pause] How does he know? Tap your guess.

Four tools watch the sky. [pause] The thermometer measures temperature, in degrees Fahrenheit. The barometer measures air pressure. The anemometer measures wind speed. And the rain gauge catches and measures rain.

One reading tells you little. But write the readings down every day, and <emphasis>patterns</emphasis> appear. [pause] Look — the pressure has fallen five days in a row. Falling pressure hints a storm is coming.
That is what a forecast is: the pattern in the records, pointed at tomorrow. [pause] Evidence at work — not magic, and not a promise.

Sometimes the sky turns fierce: thunderstorms, hurricanes, droughts — and the tornado that carried Dorothy away. [pause] Extreme weather reshapes ecosystems: grass flattened, trees down, ponds dry. [pause] When the siren sounds, people go <emphasis>down</emphasis> — into the storm cellar.

And here is the big idea. <emphasis>Weather</emphasis> is one day's sky. <emphasis>Climate</emphasis> is the pattern over many, many years. [pause] Kansas prairie summers are usually hot and dry — that is climate — even if today it rains.
Uncle Henry's barn wall. [pause] Tap what each tool measures.
Tools mastered! [pause] Now read a real record.
Here are five days of measurements from the farm. [pause] What is the best forecast for tomorrow? Use the pattern as evidence.
You read the record like a forecaster! [pause] Next: weather, or climate?
Drag each sentence to <emphasis>weather</emphasis> — one day's sky — or <emphasis>climate</emphasis> — the pattern over many years. Or tap a bin.
Sorted! [pause] Last one — storm smarts.
The sky turns dangerous. [pause] Tap the safe choice — like Dorothy should have.
Tools, records, sorting, safety — you are ready. [pause] Show what you know!
Not quite. Look at what the tool is built to catch, or feel.
Not quite. A forecast is not a coin flip — the record <emphasis>is</emphasis> evidence. What is the pressure doing?
Not quite. Careful — a forecast says <emphasis>likely</emphasis>, never for certain.
Not quite. Ask: is this one day's sky, or the pattern over many years?
Not quite. One cold week does not mean the climate changed — climate is the pattern over <emphasis>many</emphasis> years.
Not safe! In a dangerous storm, get low and get inside.
Yes! Temperature, in degrees Fahrenheit.
Yes! Air pressure — and falling pressure hints storms.
Yes! Its spinning cups catch the wind — wind speed.
Yes! It catches rain so you can measure how much fell.
Yes! Five days of falling pressure — the record points to a storm.
Yes! High, steady pressure — the record points to fair weather.
Yes! One day's sky — weather.
Yes! The pattern over many years — climate.
Yes! One event on one day — weather.
Yes! Many years measured — climate.
Yes! Even a whole cold week is still weather — the climate pattern takes many years to change.
Yes! Down and inside — just like Dorothy's storm cellar.
Yes! Inside is safest — lightning looks for tall things.
Which tool measures air pressure?
The record shows the pressure falling for two days. Tomorrow will most likely be what?
What <emphasis>is</emphasis> a forecast?
Kansas prairie summers are usually hot and dry. What does that sentence describe?
One freezing cold week arrives in May. What does it mean?
<soft>You can read the sky like a forecaster!</soft> [pause] Well done.
Good try! Let's look at the tools and records once more.
Lesson done! Now go find out how a real tornado forms — and reread your own weather journal.
